Tangling in the watercress crossing — one birch-bark hull dragging a green curtain of it broadside across the channel, a second shoving through the trailing stems with both fae rowing chest-deep in leaf, a third vaulting clean over the mat on a gust, a fourth slipping through the gap the bark hull tore open; a single mayfly hangs watching, broad as a racing fae is tall.

Dropping nose-first off the twig weir — the leading walnut shell buried to its rim in white water, one fae flat along the keel, a second hull catching air behind it and landing hard to port, a third still at the lip with its grass line dragging, a fourth riding a detached oak leaf down the slick face like a brown raft; the oak leaf wider than three hulls together.

Heeling right over on a squall — one petal sail, scarlet, flattened until its acorn hull nearly kisses the surface, a fae leaning far out off the windward rail to save it, a second boat spilling its plum petal loose and flopping bare-masted, a third rowing hard and low through the tilting field; a snail on the near bank keeps pace and, implacably, draws ahead.

Spinning stern-first in the eddy below the grey pebble — one fae digging a reed paddle against the curl to bring the hazelnut hull round, a second boat threading the eddy's outer lip in marigold sail, a third shooting through on the fast tongue inside them, a fourth backed off hard waiting; the pebble stands over the whole field like a slate cliff-face.

Overtaking under the bank with a petal sail brushing the reeds — one copper-skinned bark hull sliding through a gap barely its own width, the fae at its twig mast bent low under the fronds, a second hull crowding it from the channel side in berry-red, a third holding the racing line ahead blissfully unaware, a fourth closing fast behind with marigold sail cracked full; a reed stem rises taller than any mast in the field.

Lashed together shooting the narrow chute — two hazelnut shells bound at the gunwales with grass cord and rammed through side-by-side in a crash of white spray, the binding parting at the bottom and both hulls surging apart in opposite arcs, a third squeezing the gap a heartbeat behind them, a fourth already through and pulling clear into the sunlit pool; tucked under one thwart, a bronze-backed beetle rides the whole thing out perfectly still.

A duckling's wake rolling through the middle of the field — one bark hull lifted clean over the crest and coming down running with its cream petal sail cracking like a struck leaf, two acorn caps bailing furiously in the trough behind it, a third boat capsized and its fae riders hauling the grass lines to right it, a fourth skidding sideways across the top of the second wave; a floating oak leaf drifts past, broad as the three bailing boats laid end to end.

Bailing emergency at full speed — one moss-green shell riding low with a fae scooping water over the side stroke by stroke using an acorn cap in each hand, a second hull coming up fast on its windward quarter in deep plum sail, a third cutting inside it through the shallows, a fourth watching from behind with its oars raised to read the gap; the boot-shaped seed-pod hull sheds a thin silver arc of water with every fling.

A blown-petal squall blinding the leaders — a sudden gust of wild-cherry petals, white and cream, plastering across three petal sails at once and blinding the fae behind them, one hull swinging broadside in confusion, a second tucking its nose down and driving blind by feel alone, a third rowing bare-masted straight through the cloud into clear water with a full lead; one pink petal has lodged against a mast, unnoticed, fluttering there unnoticed the whole way down.

Mid-race repair on the move — one hazelnut hull going down by the bow while a fae slaps bark patch and pine resin over the split with flat bare hands, a second boat threading past on the port side in scarlet petal sail, a third bumping its hull against the stricken one to help and then thinking better of it and pulling away, a fourth already round the bend; a bulrush rises at the outside of the turn, taller than every mast in the field combined.

Two hulls grinding round the inside of the bend — one berry-red bark hull and one copper acorn hull locked beam-to-beam, their fae riders pushing off each other with feet braced on the opposite gunwale, neither giving a thumb's width, a third boat slipping the outside arc in marigold sail with water piling under its bow, a fourth tucking under the bank behind it; the turn is marked by a single rowanberry on a grass thread, bobbing in the churn.

A hull built too tall rolling clean over on the first crossing current — the tall birch-bark shell toppling slowly and then all at once, its fae flinging themselves onto the upturned keel, a second boat swerving wide around the wreck in cream petal sail, a third cutting inside the gap left open, a fourth stopping momentarily to stare and losing three boat-lengths to the decision; the hull lies bottom-up, and tied beneath its thwart a walnut-shell bailer still full of stolen water.

A paddle snapped clean in the eddy — one fae rowing on with a broad sycamore seed-wing held two-fisted, taking half-strokes in frantic circles to hold line, a second hull gliding past in plum sail with its fae wearing the expression of someone trying not to laugh, a third coming from behind fast in scarlet, a fourth jostling for the gap the broken stroke opened; the sycamore wing flexes with every pull and threatens to fold completely.

Racing bare-masted after a gust stripped the sail — one hazelnut hull driving on oars alone after its marigold petal sail is carried thirty lengths downstream, a second boat sheeting home a new sail, a moth wing with its amber eyespot showing, hung from a fresh twig mast at full speed, a third pulling clear in the lead, a fourth tangled in the fallen sail and dragging it like a cloak; the moth-wing sail trembles in the air and holds.

The tow going wrong — a grass line binding two hulls together snaps, the forward boat leaping ahead in a sudden surge of plum sail, the towed hull lurching back and spinning sideways into the path of a third, which swerves so hard its fae slides to the outer rail, a fourth cutting between all three with an opportunist grin; the snapped line coils on the surface a moment, then the current takes it.

Launching from the bank in a ragged shove — three hulls shoved into the stream almost together, one already crabbing sideways in the current, one straight and rowing hard in scarlet petal sail, one tangled in a reed stem with a fae pushing off it with both boots, a fourth already ten lengths ahead from an earlier start and looking back with clear satisfaction; the reed stem is as thick as that fae is tall.

Dead level in the last stretch — two shell hulls clicking oars together stroke for stroke under a marigold sail and a plum sail, a third driving under the bank with its sail let flat out in cream, its hull hidden in shadow, a fourth limping behind with a moss patch on its bow and losing ground it cannot get back; knotted to one bow, a clover head left from the last wreath ceremony drags a thin green wake.

Shooting through the twig gate neck and neck — two birch-bark hulls going through the bent-twig arch side by side with their oars overlapping in the gap, a fae on each boat pulling the crossed oar free mid-stroke, a third hull ramming the arch from behind and carrying the whole twig gate away on its bow, a fourth lifting its oars clear to wait; the arch leaves a bright green smear of lichen across the winning bow.

Capsized on the bend and hauling back — three fae knee-deep in the current righting their walnut hull on its grass lines, one already inside it bailing with an acorn cap while the others still push, a second boat swerving so wide around them it clips the far bank, a third shooting through the inside of the gap in deep scarlet sail, a fourth coming on hard behind; a water-vole watches from a root hollow, nose going, wholly unbothered.

A stowaway shifting the balance — the lightest hull in the field, a single curled birch-bark sliver, pulling clear of everything in plum sail while its fae looks puzzled by the speed, the five heavier boats working hard behind in the shade, a second hull edging close enough to see what is wrong, a third closing from the bank side; under the stern thwart a broad-backed river beetle rides out the whole race in perfect stillness.

A reed sweeping the leading mast clean — the front hull losing its twig mast and cream petal sail to a low-hanging frond in one silent swipe, both spinning end over end into the water ahead of the boat, the fae catching the mast stub and staring at it, a second hull threading between the wreckage and the bank in marigold, a third taking the mast clean in the chest and being knocked back into a fourth hull coming up hard; the fern frond hangs over the channel like a green vaulted roof and nobody warned anyone.

Surfing the fallen leaf over the twig weir — the leading fae balanced upright on a broad, drifting sycamore leaf, its walnut hull nested in the leaf's curl, the whole assembly riding the slick face of a twig dam in a smooth curving rush, a second hull trying the same move and catching its bow on the twig lip, a third portaging around the end of the dam in furious haste, a fourth watching from upstream and biding its time; the sycamore leaf is wide as the whole channel to everyone watching.

A blown-grass line fouling three hulls at the bend — one long strand of parted grass cord wrapping itself round an acorn hull's twig oar, trailing back to catch a second boat's bow, the third boat piling in behind it and all three slewing together, the fae on each reaching for the cord in the same moment and finding the others already there, a fourth threading the chaos in berry-red sail with its fae flat on the thwart; the whole tangle revolves slowly on the current and refuses to simplify.

Overtaking through a shaft of light — one copper bark hull breaking out of the shadow into a brilliant fall of sun, its marigold sail flaring gold from grey to blinding in a single hull-length, two more boats still labouring in the shade behind a watercress bridge, a fourth coming from the shadow on the other side in plum sail, both reaching for the same bright water; a dragonfly hovers in the shaft, wide as the hull is long, wholly absorbed in its own business.

A walnut shell spun by the eddy and rowed round again — its fae digging both leaf-oars in desperate asymmetric strokes to bring the bow back downstream, a second hull passing it broadside-on in scarlet petal sail with a fae calling something the noise of the water covers completely, a third shooting past on the inside in cream, a fourth approaching the same eddy with visible apprehension and taking the long way round losing two lengths to caution; the walnut hull completes its full circle and emerges going slightly faster than before.

Tangling in the watercress bridge — one birch-bark hull dragging a green beard of it sideways across the channel, a second slipping under the trailing fronds by lying its mast flat, a third fae standing in her acorn shell hacking stems with a flint chip, while the fourth bores through trailing the whole clump behind, winning nothing, decorated absurdly.

Dropping nose-first over the twig weir — the leading walnut shell buried to its thwarts in white foam, two slender fae flat on their faces gripping the rim, a second hull riding the back of a broad oak leaf over the lip like a board, a third hesitating above with oars lifted, a single bulrush rising behind the whole field taller than any mast.

Spinning stern-first in the eddy below the grey boulder — one hazelnut shell going round for the second time, its fae rowing in furious circles, a second boat jabbing a reed-stem into the bed to pivot clear, a third slipping past on the outside and not looking back, a rowanberry turn-marker bobbing on its grass line watching the whole embarrassment.

A squall of blown cherry petals blinding the leaders — two acorn hulls slewing broadside with petals plastered over every sail, a fae on the third peeling them off her face with one hand and rowing with the other, the fourth boring through with its leaf sail shut tight as a fist and stealing twenty lengths in the confusion.

Lashing together to shoot the narrow chute — two birch-bark hulls roped side by side with a braid of grass cord, both fae leaning inward as they accelerate, a third hull watching from above the lip and measuring the gap, the lashed pair coming apart at the bottom with a crack and surging in opposite directions, one acorn cap spinning away across the foam.

A line snapping mid-tow — the lead hazelnut shell lunging forward so hard its bow lifts clear of the water, the towed acorn hull rocketing backwards into the path of a third, a fourth swerving so wide its petal sail brushes the underside of a fern frond overhanging the whole field like a green roof, and the fae holding the broken grass end staring at it.

Overtaking under the far bank — a slim birch-bark hull slipping between the reeds and the third-place acorn shell, its moth-wing sail bent almost flat against the stems, a fae on the overtaken boat leaning out to block with her paddle and missing, a tiny snail keeping exact pace along the mud of the bank and sitting ahead of them both at the end of the stroke.

Bailing in full race — an acorn shell riding so low its bow-fae scoops water with the hull's own cap while the stern-fae rows alone and still gains, a second boat running dry past them with a look of pure scorn, a third shipping a wave from a coot's kick and starting the same desperate business, a fourth already through and dwindling to a berry-red dot.

Heeling hard over in the gust — one petal sail laid flat to the water, its fae out along the windward hull-edge on one pointed foot, the hull's own reflection pressed against it like a mirror, a second spilling its sail deliberately and dropping to oars, a third riding the same gust perfectly and pulling clear, an oak leaf drifting past wider than three boats together.

Hull holed and going down by the bow — a walnut shell tipping forward in slow horror, its fae standing in the stern to keep weight aft, neighbours on both sides peeling away hard, a third cutting inside through the gap the sinking makes, the stricken fae already slapping a curl of pine-resin bark over the split with her palm flat against it.

Launching from the bank in a ragged scramble — hulls shoved into the current one after another, two acorn shells colliding before they have gone a body-length, a hazelnut stern still touching the mud while its fae shoves with a reed, a fourth already three lengths clear and its scarlet petal sail filling, the start called by a single thump on an upturned acorn-cap drum still ringing.

Riding a broad sycamore wing over the fallen-twig weir — one folded-leaf hull surfing the flat of it, perfectly balanced, the fae inside upright and arms wide in disbelief, a second hull missing the wing entirely and crashing through the foam below, a third punting itself over on a twig-pole, the wing-rider skimming clear a full boat-length ahead by the time it reaches flat water.

A wave from a waddling duckling swamping the middle of the field — three hulls awash at once, acorn-cap bailers flashing in every direction, one rolling completely over while its fae clings to the grass lines underneath, a fourth lifted over the wave's back and landing running, its broad sycamore-wing sail cracking taut, the duckling padding on in total ignorance of the devastation.

Two hulls locked side-on at the inside of the bend — grinding round together, neither giving, both fae braced foot-to-foot across the gap between them, a third slipping outside on a wide arc under a cream flower-petal sail streaked with one violet line, a fourth using the locked pair as a wall to pivot off and shooting through the gap below them clean.

Mid-race sail repair at full speed — a fae re-lashing her torn meadowsweet-petal sail to its twig mast with a strip of grass cord held in her teeth and both hands, the hull running bare-masted and falling back, two boats passing her on the left, one closing from behind whose fae is leaning forward watching every knot she ties with unconcealed interest.

Cutting the corner through the watercress — a hazelnut hull ploughing a green furrow through it, stems wrapped round the bow like a necklace, gaining the inside of the bend but slowing to nearly nothing, a second boat taking the clean line and sliding past, a third following the furrow the first has cut and moving faster through it, the clever thought arriving one boat too late.

A hull built too tall rolling clean over on the first cross-current — marigold petal sail going straight down into the water, its fae thrown out sideways into the stream, the capsized hull now the flattest and fastest object on the water, skimming hull-up while a passing dragonfly the size of a rowing fae regards it with enormous compound eyes and continues on its way.

A stowaway beetle found mid-race to be the reason the lightest hull is three lengths clear — the fae looking down at him wedged under the stern thwart, the beetle looking back, both of them going very fast, the second-place walnut shell's fae having put this together and already protesting to a fat frog sitting steady on a lily pad at the turn.

Paddle snapped clean at the neck — the snapped half spinning away into the current, the fae rowing on with a broad sycamore leaf held in both hands, blades dripping, losing ground but fighting, two hulls passing in a rush of berry-red and plum, a fourth drawing alongside and its fae holding out a spare reed-stem with an expression of maximum reluctant charity.

Piling into the pebble gate three abreast — one acorn hull climbing the grey stone's face, its fae running up the curve of it like a tiny acrobat, two more hulls pressing in below and jamming fast, the fourth threading the outer gap in a single clean move under a moth-wing sail with its eyespot catching the light, a river pebble standing over the whole scene like a cliff.

An eddy spinning one shell stern-first and the fae deciding to row backwards for the turn — going round the rowanberry marker perfectly, stern leading, with tremendous accidental style, passing a fae on a second hull who has stopped rowing entirely to watch, a third taking the turn correctly and conventionally and somehow looking worse, the fae in the backwards shell giving a small seated bow to no one in particular.

Shooting a rapid nose-down in sheets of white — a birch-bark hull half buried, its copper-painted side just visible through the foam, two fae gripping the thwarts with all four hands, a second hull dropping in behind before the first has cleared, a third still above the lip watching the chaos with its plum petal sail shivering, a strand of watercress crossing the channel below the pool like a low finishing bridge.

Two boats luffing into each other at the rowanberry turn — their twig masts crossing overhead with a dry knock, petal sails of scarlet and gold tangled at the tips, both fae leaning out and pushing the masts apart with straight arms, a third threading between their trailing grass lines with a fae lying flat on the hull to duck under, a fourth simply running them both wide and taking the inside.

A hull catching air off the lip of a submerged pebble — going fully airborne for one long fae-breath, its moss-green shell dark against the sky, the fae's copper hair streaming straight up, the hull landing flat with a smack that sends a ring of droplets wide, a second hull hitting the same stone and not getting air and simply stopping dead, which is somehow worse.

Reeds closing across the fast channel — one acorn hull threading through with its twig mast tilted sideways, a second trying the gap a moment late and wedging its bow between two stems, its fae pushing both stems apart with a foot on each, a third turning back and taking the slow water outside, a strand of dandelion-down strung low between two reeds marking the channel's end, every seed still intact.

The whole field overtaken from behind by the one who repaired her hull — a bark-patched birch shell coming through on the left with its plum petal sail cracked out full, passing the second boat, passing the first, the fae on the leaders checking over their shoulders in pure horror, the bark patch still wet, the pine resin still dark, a mayfly the size of the rowing fae watching from a stem above.

Two hulls riding one oak leaf together down a glassy chute — the leaf bending along its own midrib, one hull on each lobe, the two fae looking sideways at each other with the specific expression of people sharing a very small problem, a third boat waiting above the chute with both fae's arms crossed, having correctly decided this is someone else's terrible idea.

The last turn taken so hard a hull skids sideways — its petal sail slapping the water and throwing spray ten fae-heights in the air, the skid carrying it wide and giving two lengths to the hazelnut shell coming inside, the skidding fae recovering and bearing away in the new direction, the tail of the field appearing round the bend behind them all, the clover-garland finish suddenly close.

A gust taking the lead sail clean off its twig mast — the whole marigold petal tumbling downwind across the water like a falling sun, both fae on the leading hull watching it go, the second boat sailing straight under it, becoming briefly golden as it drapes across them and then slides into the stream, the third and fourth boats rowing past the mast-fae who is already unlashing a spare moth-wing from under the thwart.

Stacking against the rowanberry turn-marker — a hazelnut shell grinding broadside into a walnut hull, both spinning together, a birch-bark slipper shooting the gap inside with its moth-wing sail cracking, a fourth backing hard on its reed oars, a snail on the marker-stone keeping steadier pace than any of them.

Pitching nose-first down the twig-weir chute — the leading acorn hull buried to its thwarts in white froth, two slender fae flat in the bow with their leaf-cloth cloaks soaked through, a second dropping in behind, a third hovering at the lip with its oars shipped, a single bulrush rising taller than every mast in the waiting field.

Heeling hard over in the downstream squall of blown cherry petals — one petal sail flattened pink-over-pink until the hull lies on its ear, a fae in moss-velvet hanging far out over the water as counterweight, a second boat spilling its scarlet sail loose to run bare, a third driving straight through blind, its pilot's bright wings spread wide for balance.

Swamped broadside by the rolling wake of a passing duckling — two walnut shells awash to their thwarts, a fae in each bailing in furious strokes with upturned acorn caps, a third hull lifted clean over the crest and landing at full run, a fourth already a length clear and pulling away into the calm, its marigold petal sail unmarked.

Cutting the watercress corner — one bark sliver slicing through the green tangle and dragging a long ragged plume of it off the bank, a fae in plum leaf-cloth hacking at the trailing stems with a sharp twig, two rivals holding the clean channel and gaining a boat-length each, the watercress strand itself bridging the whole channel like a low green roof.

Caught broadside in the eddy behind the grey boulder — a hazelnut shell spinning helplessly stern-first, its fae pilot rowing one side then the other in furious bursts, a walnut hull steering wide to avoid it, a birch-bark racer threading between them at full drive, a stowaway beetle clinging under the lead boat's thwart making it the lightest and fastest in the field.

Capsized on the fast bend — four fae in petal-silk hauling their shell hull back upright by its grass-cord lines, one already aboard bailing with a cupped acorn cap while water sheets over the side, two plum-sailed rivals swerving wide, a third stealing inside through the reeds, a fallen oak leaf drifting past wider than three boats laid end to end.

Holed by the gravel bar and going down bow-first — one bark hull tipping steep, its fae slapping a pine-resin patch over the split with both hands while a copper-hulled rival swerves hard away, a third drives straight past without mercy, a fourth fae leans out with pebbles in each fist to count the gap at the gravel marker.

Lashed together at the top of the chute — two shells bound side-by-side with braided grass cord shooting the rapid as one wide raft, all four fae flat and grinning, the cord snapping at the bottom and both hulls surging apart into different channels, a mayfly rising off the foam exactly the size of a rowing fae.

A paddle snapped clean at the throat — the fae left holding a bare twig stub, snatching a broad sycamore leaf from the water and rowing on with it held in both hands, the boat losing ground stroke by stroke while a marigold-sailed rival sweeps past, a moss-green hull two lengths behind closing fast with its own oars pulling long and even.

Riding a curled sycamore leaf over the twig-weir like a board — the lead hull surfing down the curl at frightening speed, its fae pilot crouched low with wings tucked tight in copper-coloured cloth, a second boat dropping in too late and spinning, a third going over the side of the weir altogether, a river pebble standing over the whole scene like a grey tower.

Re-hanging a sail at full speed — a fae in scarlet moss-velvet clinging halfway up a twig mast with the petal held in her teeth, the hull yawing across the current while two rivals drive past to port and starboard, a fourth boat sailing serenely clear on its moth-wing sail, its eyespot catching the light like a single watching eye.

Tow-line snapping mid-rapid — both fae hurled back as the braided grass cord parts, the towed hull surging ahead suddenly faster than the tower, two rival acorn shells scattering from the gap between them, a fourth threading through the chaos untouched, a single dandelion-seed drifting down onto the towed hull's bow and snagging there as an accidental second sail.

Launching in a ragged line from the mossy bank — hulls shoved into the current one after another, two fae tangling their oars on the first stroke, a third already pulling clear with a scarlet petal sail catching the first breath of air, a fourth spinning hull-first downstream before its pilot has both oars seated, all dwarfed by a single overhanging fern frond wide enough to roof the field.

Bailing at full race-pace — a fae in leaf-cloth bailing with an acorn cap in one hand and rowing with the other, the hull still moving, its plum petal sail still drawing, a walnut rival pulling clear beside it, a third boat coming up hard from behind, a fourth fae balanced on the bow of the sinking hull shifting every scrap of pine-resin ballast aft.

Two hulls dead-level in the last reach — oars touching stroke for stroke, a marigold sail against a scarlet one, both crews' wings rigid and flat with effort, a third hull storming up in the bank's shadow with its broad-veined leaf sail let all the way out, a strand of linked clover heads strung between two reeds trembling at the run's end ahead.

Spinning stern-first in the big eddy below the stone — a fae rowing herself around again in desperate circles, wings flared for balance in a leaf-green tunic, a copper hull sweeping past on the outside, a third cracking through the middle, a fourth pausing just long enough for its fae pilot to drop a fresh pebble on the twig-tally at the eddy's edge.

A hull built too wide rolling clean over at the first bend — its fae tumbling into the current, wings spread flat on the surface, catching the trailing grass-cord and righting the shell hand over hand, a marigold rival steering carefully wide, a third cutting inside and clipping the capsized hull with its copper bow, a fourth lifting over the wreck's wake and pressing on.

Threading the bent-twig gate sideways — one hazelnut hull crabbing through at an angle with millimetres to spare, its fae in plum petal-cloth cringing inward, a second hull grinding the twig with a sound like a struck seed-pod, a third pulling perfectly straight through the centre, a fat frog sitting solid on the downstream pebble watching the turn with both golden eyes wide.

A sudden gust taking only the leaders — the front two hulls heeling hard until their moth-wing and marigold sails drag their tips in the water, a third boat rowing bare-masted straight through the gusting pair, a fourth behind shaking out its fold-veined leaf sail to catch the same wind, a single bulrush swaying its brown head across the whole width of the channel.

Overtaking hard under the bank with the reed-heads brushing a petal sail — the inside fae lying almost flat to clear them, a marigold sail streaked with green pollen, the boat she is passing grinding its oars against the clay and losing half a stroke, two more hulls behind in the open channel trading water for speed, one shipping a full acorn cup of stream over its bow.

Piling three deep against the grey midstream stone — the first hull pinned flat, its fae shoving at the stone with both feet in bark-soled slippers, a second grinding in behind and locking them tighter, a third sweeping round the outside clean into the lead, a fourth holding off with oars braced wide, its scarlet petal sail still full and pulling.

A stowaway beetle shifting its weight at the critical moment — the lightest hull in the field tilting its bow up a finger's width and gaining half a stroke on the tack, a copper-sailed rival drawing alongside, a walnut shell one length back labouring with too much ballast, all four closing on a rowanberry turn-marker bobbing on its grass-cord tether in the stream.

Blinded by a downstream squall of blown apple petals — the leaders driving on with eyes shut and wings tucked, a cream petal sail indistinguishable in the white cloud of them, two boats in the thick of the field swerving for opposite banks, a third rowing by feel alone, a heron standing motionless over the far bend watching all of it through one copper eye.

A mid-race repair on the move — pine resin slapped onto a split strake with a bark-chip patch pressed hard over it, the fae in moss-cloth holding it with her knee while her hull drifts, two rivals pulling ahead, a third slowing to look and then thinking better of it, an oak leaf wider than three boats drifting past and briefly tipping the patched hull as it goes.

Two hulls bumping and grinding round the inside of the fast bend — locked in a creak of shell on bark, both pilots bracing with an oar each, their scarlet and plum sails tangled at their tips, a third hull slipping through the wide outside arc and coming out first, a fourth fae standing in the stern of the wreck counting the gap with pebbles on a twig.

A boot-shaped seed-pod shipping water in the chop — bailed with frantic tilts of an acorn cap, the fae in copper leaf-cloth rowing and bailing in alternating strokes, a walnut hull overtaking it easily, a birch-bark racer cutting inside both of them, all three vanishing under a fern frond arched over the channel like the roof of a great hall.

A mouse towed in a walnut fragment as ballast weight — the line going taut on every gust and throwing the lead hull off-line, a second fae in plum cloth drawing level and holding it, a third cutting inside at the reeds, the mouse sitting calm through all of it, its tail a thin rudder dragging in the current, a mayfly lifting off the bow exactly its size.

A stowaway moth-wing sail shaken out at the halfway stone — a fae producing the shed wing from inside her leaf-cloth jacket and bending it to the twig mast at full drift, gaining three strokes before the others notice, two rivals already past the rowanberry mark watching over their shoulders, a fourth hull still wrestling the mark's eddy with its oars braced across the stream.

Dead level with three hulls touching at the clover garland end-strand — a scarlet petal sail, a marigold one and a broad-veined leaf sail all driving together through the same linked clover heads, the strand parting across all three bows at once, a fourth fae arriving a breath later slamming both oars flat on the water to stop from running through the lot of them.

Tangling into the watercress bridge — a copper-bark hull dragging a whole green curtain of it behind like a bridal train, a second fae hacking at the stems with a flint sliver while her boat slows, two more threading the clear gap to the right, a walnut shell already through and pulling away, a mayfly lifting off beside the leaders, its wings as wide as their hulls.

Pitching nose-down through the rapid — the leading acorn-cap hull buried to the thwart in white curl, one slender fae flat across the bow with her leaf-cloth sleeves streaming, a second boat angled sideways catching the chute wrong and spinning, a third dropping in perfectly behind the first, a folded-bark vessel still up on the lip with both oars dug back hard.

Caught broadside by the petal squall — a scarlet poppy sail folded flat until the hull beneath it tilts its keel to the sky, its fae crew a single pointed-eared figure hanging from the mast-twig by both fists, two boats already stripped bare-masted and rowing through the blizzard of pink petals, a fourth surfing the gust with a moth-wing sail crackling taut, a single river pebble behind the field standing over everything like a grey tower.

Riding the fallen-twig weir — a hazelnut shell hull surfing clean over the lip on a dead oak leaf curled like a dish, both crew fae whooping, their wings flattened in the rush, a birch-bark vessel dropping too early and broaching sideways in the foam, two more jostling for the line above the weir where a bulrush stem rises taller than any mast they carry.

Spun stern-first in the great eddy — a walnut-shell hull going round and round, its fae working one oar in frantic circles, pointed ears flat with effort, while a berry-red bark slab shoots past laughing, a second vessel dips an acorn cap to bail what the eddy threw aboard, and a fourth peels out of the swirl into clean current, a tiny spiral of stolen waterweed still corkscrewing off its stern.

Lashed together through the narrows — two acorn hulls bound side-by-side with plaited grass cord, their four fae rowing in ragged unison, the whole double-boat just barely fitting the gap between two pebbles, while a third vessel squeezes outside them along the moss, a fourth hanging back with oars raised waiting, the gap between the pebbles barely wider than one fallen oak leaf laid flat.

The tow-line snapping — both fae crews flung backward as the grass cord parts, the towing walnut shell leaping forward and nearly burying its bow, the towed birch-bark slab stuttering to a near-stop, two rivals surging past on either flank like copper and plum arrows, and one tiny passenger — a rove-beetle wedged under the towed boat's thwart — the only one aboard who saw it coming.

Holed and going down — a split acorn hull settling by the bow while its fae presses a pine-resin patch and a strip of bark against the crack with both knees, water silver across the floor, two moss-green vessels swerving wide around the wreck, a third cutting hard inside barely a beetle-length clear, the whole sinking drama happening in the shadow of one overhanging fern frond as wide as the entire channel.

Shooting clear into the bright shaft — a marigold-petal-sailed boat pulling suddenly from shadow into a column of gold light, its hull blazing copper, both crew fae blinking, while the three vessels behind them still labour dark in the shade, one fae raising a hand against the glare, and a dragonfly hovering at the edge of the light-shaft like a jewelled gate-keeper, real wings rigid, real compound eyes forward.

The duckling wave hitting the field — a passing duckling's bow-wake lifting three hulls at once, one walnut shell rolling clean over, a plum-petal sail going underwater and then bursting back up streaming, two fae bailing with cupped acorn caps as fast as their wrists will move, a fourth boat ridden right up over the crest of the wave and landing flat and running, its scarlet sail cracking like a struck drum.

Cutting the corner through the reeds — a slim birch-bark hull pushing into the reed-stems on the inside of the bend, its single amber-winged fae lying almost flat to thread the gap, a marigold-sailed rival taking the wide clean line and going faster for it, two more boats locked wheel-to-wheel on the bend's spine, and one reed stem swinging back to flick the birch-bark hull precisely amidships as it passes.

Two hulls grinding round the bend — a moss-green acorn shell and a berry-red bark slab pressed together side-on, their oar-shafts crossed and sparring, both sets of fae leaning in and shoving with their feet, a third vessel already through and into clear water ahead, a fourth slipping around the outside with a cream petal sail curved full and taut, a snail on the inner bank keeping unhurried pace with the whole grinding tangle and gaining.

Bailing at racing speed — a copper-hulled acorn cap so low in the water it leaves a wake of its own displacement, one fae rowing with her whole body while the other flings water overboard with a second acorn cap cupped in both hands, a plum-sailed rival drawing level and then past, a third boat briefly slowing to look and its crew catching themselves and sprinting on, a fourth already three lengths gone.

Launching ragged from the bank — six hulls shoved into the current one after another, two still touching, oars tangled, one acorn cap spinning broadside to the flow before its fae hauls it straight, a moss boat already stroking hard while its fae crew of two snap their tiny leaf-cloth cloaks back over their wings, and the very last hull pushed off so hard it slides under the lead boat's stern-line and both crews shriek.

The capsize hauled upright — three fae up to their chests in current, dragging a walnut shell back over by its grass lines, wings useless and flat against their backs, water streaming from every twig-rib, one already inside and bailing, while two scarlet-sailed rivals swing wide around the wreck, a third taking the inside so close its oar-tip catches the capsized hull and sends a small silver ring of water across the surface.

A sail unbent and re-strung at speed — one fae standing upright in a rocking hazelnut hull, threading a fresh moth-wing sail — grey-and-amber with a single natural eyespot — onto the mast-twig with fingers that are also keeping balance, the hull swaying dangerously, two boats already past and one closing hard, a walnut shell bumping the swaying hull's side in passing and not even pausing, a dandelion seed caught on the bare twig just before the new sail goes up.
